claim: Mutations in the α2 helix of the motor domain of KIF22 have been identified in patients with abnormal skeletal development.
source: Mutations in the α2 helix of the motor domain of KIF22 have been identified in patients with abnormal skeletal development, and we report the identification of a patient with a novel mutation in the KIF22 tail.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to prior work (Boyden et al., 2011; Min et al., 2011; Tüysüz et al., 2015) in the introduction.

claim: A novel mutation in the KIF22 tail (V475G) was identified in a patient.
source: Mutations in the α2 helix of the motor domain of KIF22 have been identified in patients with abnormal skeletal development, and we report the identification of a patient with a novel mutation in the KIF22 tail.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, and the results section provides clinical and genetic data for the patient with the V475G mutation.

claim: Pathogenic mutations in KIF22 do not result in a loss of KIF22's functions in early mitosis.
source: We demonstrate that pathogenic mutations do not result in a loss of KIF22's functions in early mitosis.
evidence: The abstract states this conclusion, which is supported by experimental data showing that mutant KIF22 localizes normally and generates polar ejection forces in prometaphase and metaphase.

claim: Pathogenic mutations in KIF22 disrupt chromosome segregation in anaphase.
source: Instead, mutations disrupt chromosome segregation in anaphase, resulting in reduced proliferation, abnormal daughter cell nuclear morphology, and, in a subset of cells, cytokinesis failure.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by live-cell imaging data showing chromosome recongression in anaphase in cells expressing mutant KIF22.

claim: Expression of mutant KIF22 results in reduced proliferation.
source: Instead, mutations disrupt chromosome segregation in anaphase, resulting in reduced proliferation, abnormal daughter cell nuclear morphology, and, in a subset of cells, cytokinesis failure.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by proliferation assay data showing reduced growth rates in cells expressing mutant KIF22.

claim: Expression of mutant KIF22 results in abnormal daughter cell nuclear morphology.
source: Instead, mutations disrupt chromosome segregation in anaphase, resulting in reduced proliferation, abnormal daughter cell nuclear morphology, and, in a subset of cells, cytokinesis failure.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by nuclear solidity measurements showing lobed and fragmented nuclei in cells expressing mutant KIF22.

claim: Expression of mutant KIF22 results in cytokinesis failure in a subset of cells.
source: Instead, mutations disrupt chromosome segregation in anaphase, resulting in reduced proliferation, abnormal daughter cell nuclear morphology, and, in a subset of cells, cytokinesis failure.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by live-cell imaging data showing that approximately 25-36% of cells expressing mutant KIF22 fail to complete cytokinesis.

claim: The phenotype of pathogenic mutations could be explained by a failure of KIF22 to inactivate in anaphase.
source: This phenotype could be explained by a failure of KIF22 to inactivate in anaphase.
evidence: The abstract states this interpretation, which is supported by the observation that constitutive activation of KIF22 phenocopies the effects of pathogenic mutations.

claim: Constitutive activation of KIF22 via phosphorylation at T463 phenocopies the effects of pathogenic mutations.
source: Consistent with this model, constitutive activation of the motor via a known site of phosphoregulation in the tail phenocopied the effects of pathogenic mutations.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by experimental data showing that KIF22-GFP T463D causes anaphase chromosome recongression and nuclear morphology defects similar to those seen with pathogenic mutations.

claim: The motor domain α2 helix may be an important site for regulation of KIF22 activity at the metaphase to anaphase transition.
source: These results suggest that the motor domain α2 helix may be an important site for regulation of KIF22 activity at the metaphase to anaphase transition.
evidence: The abstract states this interpretation, which is supported by the observation that pathogenic mutations in the α2 helix disrupt anaphase chromosome segregation.

claim: Mimicking phosphorylation of α2 helix residue T158 prevents inactivation of KIF22 in anaphase.
source: In support of this conclusion, mimicking phosphorylation of α2 helix residue T158 also prevents inactivation of KIF22 in anaphase.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by experimental data showing that KIF22-GFP T158D causes anaphase chromosome recongression.

claim: KIF22 is a plus-end directed member of the kinesin-10 family.
source: The chromokinesin KIF22 (or Kid, kinesin-like DNA-binding protein) is a plus-end directed member of the kinesin-10 family (Yajima et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to Yajima et al., 2003.

claim: KIF22 generates forces that move chromosomes away from the spindle poles.
source: KIF22 and its orthologs, including Nod (Drosophila melanogaster) (Zhang et al., 1990) and Xkid (Xenopus laevis) (Antonio et al., 2000; Funabiki and Murray, 2000; Takagi et al., 2013), generate forces that move chromosomes away from the spindle poles.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: KIF22 contains a conserved kinesin motor domain responsible for ATP hydrolysis and microtubule binding.
source: Structurally, KIF22 contains a conserved kinesin motor domain responsible for ATP hydrolysis and microtubule binding (Tokai et al., 1996; Yajima et al., 2003), a second microtubule-binding domain in the tail (Shiroguchi et al., 2003), a predicted coiled-coil domain (Shiroguchi et al., 2003), and a C-terminal DNA binding domain, which includes a helix-hairpin-helix motif (Tokai et al., 1996; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work. Figure 1A shows a schematic of KIF22 domains.

claim: KIF22 contains a second microtubule-binding domain in the tail.
source: Structurally, KIF22 contains a conserved kinesin motor domain responsible for ATP hydrolysis and microtubule binding (Tokai et al., 1996; Yajima et al., 2003), a second microtubule-binding domain in the tail (Shiroguchi et al., 2003), a predicted coiled-coil domain (Shiroguchi et al., 2003), and a C-terminal DNA binding domain, which includes a helix-hairpin-helix motif (Tokai et al., 1996; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to Shiroguchi et al., 2003. Figure 1A shows a schematic of KIF22 domains.

claim: KIF22 contains a predicted coiled-coil domain.
source: Structurally, KIF22 contains a conserved kinesin motor domain responsible for ATP hydrolysis and microtubule binding (Tokai et al., 1996; Yajima et al., 2003), a second microtubule-binding domain in the tail (Shiroguchi et al., 2003), a predicted coiled-coil domain (Shiroguchi et al., 2003), and a C-terminal DNA binding domain, which includes a helix-hairpin-helix motif (Tokai et al., 1996; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to Shiroguchi et al., 2003. Figure 1A shows a schematic of KIF22 domains.

claim: KIF22 contains a C-terminal DNA binding domain, which includes a helix-hairpin-helix motif.
source: Structurally, KIF22 contains a conserved kinesin motor domain responsible for ATP hydrolysis and microtubule binding (Tokai et al., 1996; Yajima et al., 2003), a second microtubule-binding domain in the tail (Shiroguchi et al., 2003), a predicted coiled-coil domain (Shiroguchi et al., 2003), and a C-terminal DNA binding domain, which includes a helix-hairpin-helix motif (Tokai et al., 1996; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to Tokai et al., 1996. Figure 1A shows a schematic of KIF22 domains.

claim: In interphase, KIF22 localizes to the nucleus.
source: In interphase, KIF22 localizes to the nucleus (Levesque and Compton, 2001; Tokai et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: As cells enter mitosis, chromosomes condense and KIF22 binds along chromosome arms.
source: As cells enter mitosis, chromosomes condense and KIF22 binds along chromosome arms (Levesque and Compton, 2001; Tokai et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: KIF22 generates polar ejection forces that push the arms of chromosomes away from the spindle poles and toward the center of the spindle.
source: The interactions of the KIF22 motor domain with spindle microtubules and the KIF22 tail with chromosome arms allow the motor to generate polar ejection forces (Bieling et al., 2010; Brouhard and Hunt, 2005), which push the arms of chromosomes away from the spindle poles and toward the center of the spindle (Marshall et al., 2001; Rieder and Salmon, 1994; Rieder et al., 1986), contributing to chromosome congression in prometaphase (Iemura and Tanaka, 2015; Levesque and Compton, 2001; Wandke et al., 2012), as well as chromosome arm orientation (Levesque and Compton, 2001; Wandke et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Polar ejection forces contribute to chromosome congression in prometaphase.
source: The interactions of the KIF22 motor domain with spindle microtubules and the KIF22 tail with chromosome arms allow the motor to generate polar ejection forces (Bieling et al., 2010; Brouhard and Hunt, 2005), which push the arms of chromosomes away from the spindle poles and toward the center of the spindle (Marshall et al., 2001; Rieder and Salmon, 1994; Rieder et al., 1986), contributing to chromosome congression in prometaphase (Iemura and Tanaka, 2015; Levesque and Compton, 2001; Wandke et al., 2012), as well as chromosome arm orientation (Levesque and Compton, 2001; Wandke et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Polar ejection forces contribute to chromosome arm orientation.
source: The interactions of the KIF22 motor domain with spindle microtubules and the KIF22 tail with chromosome arms allow the motor to generate polar ejection forces (Bieling et al., 2010; Brouhard and Hunt, 2005), which push the arms of chromosomes away from the spindle poles and toward the center of the spindle (Marshall et al., 2001; Rieder and Salmon, 1994; Rieder et al., 1986), contributing to chromosome congression in prometaphase (Iemura and Tanaka, 2015; Levesque and Compton, 2001; Wandke et al., 2012), as well as chromosome arm orientation (Levesque and Compton, 2001; Wandke et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In metaphase, polar ejection forces contribute to chromosome oscillation and alignment.
source: In metaphase, polar ejection forces also contribute to chromosome oscillation and alignment (Antonio et al., 2000; Funabiki and Murray, 2000; Levesque and Compton, 2001; Levesque et al., 2003; Stumpff et al., 2012; Takagi et al., 2013; Tokai-Nishizumi et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Purified KIF22 is monomeric.
source: Purified KIF22 is monomeric (Shiroguchi et al., 2003; Yajima et al., 2003), and the forces generated by KIF22 on chromosomes arms may represent the collective action of many monomers.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In anaphase, KIF22 is inactivated to reduce polar ejection forces and allow chromosomes to segregate toward the spindle poles.
source: In anaphase, KIF22 is inactivated to reduce polar ejection forces and allow chromosomes to segregate toward the spindle poles (Soeda et al., 2016; Su et al., 2016; Wolf et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The generation of polar ejection forces by KIF22 is regulated by the activity of cyclin-dependent kinase 1 (CDK1)/cyclin B.
source: The generation of polar ejection forces by KIF22 is regulated by the activity of cyclin-dependent kinase 1 (CDK1)/cyclin B, which is high in prometa- and metaphase, and drops sharply at the metaphase to anaphase transition when cyclin B is degraded (Hershko, 1999; Morgan, 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: KIF22 is phosphorylated by CDK1/cyclin B at T463.
source: KIF22 is phosphorylated by CDK1/cyclin B at T463, a residue in the tail of the motor between the second microtubule-binding and coiled-coil domains.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is consistent with prior work on KIF22 phosphorylation.

claim: Phosphorylation of T463 is required for polar ejection force generation in prometa- and metaphase.
source: Phosphorylation of T463 is required for polar ejection force generation in prometa- and metaphase, and dephosphorylation of T463 is necessary for the suspension of polar ejection forces to allow chromosome segregation in anaphase (Soeda et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to Soeda et al., 2016.

claim: Dephosphorylation of T463 is necessary for the suspension of polar ejection forces to allow chromosome segregation in anaphase.
source: Phosphorylation of T463 is required for polar ejection force generation in prometa- and metaphase, and dephosphorylation of T463 is necessary for the suspension of polar ejection forces to allow chromosome segregation in anaphase (Soeda et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to Soeda et al., 2016.

claim: Phosphoproteomic studies have identified sites of phosphorylation within KIF22's α2 helix.
source: Phosphoproteomic studies have identified sites of phosphorylation within KIF22's α2 helix (Kettenbach et al., 2011; Olsen et al., 2010; Rigbolt et al., 2011), suggesting this region, in addition to the tail, may also be important for the regulation of motor activity.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Mutations in KIF22 cause the developmental disorder spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia with joint laxity, leptodactylic type (SEMDJL2).
source: Mutations in KIF22 cause the developmental disorder spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia with joint laxity, leptodactylic type (SEMDJL2, also referred to as Hall Type or lepto-SEMDJL) (Boyden et al., 2011; Min et al., 2011; Tüysüz et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Four point mutations in two amino acids have been reported in SEMDJL2 patients.
source: Four point mutations in two amino acids have been reported in SEMDJL2 patients (Boyden et al., 2011; Min et al., 2011; Tüysüz et al., 2015; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work. Figure 1A shows the locations of these mutations.

claim: SEMDJL2 mutations occur in adjacent residues P148 and R149 in the α2 helix of the KIF22 motor domain.
source: These mutations occur in adjacent residues P148 and R149 in the α2 helix of the KIF22 motor domain (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction. Figure 1B shows the location of P148 and R149 in the α2 helix.

claim: P148 and R149 are conserved in kinesin-10 family members across species.
source: P148 and R149 are conserved in kinesin-10 family members across species (Figure 1C) and in many human members of the kinesin superfamily (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction. Figure 1C shows sequence alignments demonstrating conservation of P148 and R149 in kinesin-10 family members.

claim: P148 and R149 are conserved in many human members of the kinesin superfamily.
source: P148 and R149 are conserved in kinesin-10 family members across species (Figure 1C) and in many human members of the kinesin superfamily (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction. Figure 1D shows sequence alignments demonstrating conservation of P148 and R149 in human kinesin superfamily members.

claim: All identified SEMDJL2 patients are heterozygous for a single mutation in KIF22.
source: All identified patients are heterozygous for a single mutation in KIF22.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is consistent with prior reports of SEMDJL2 patients.

claim: Mutations in KIF22 dominantly cause SEMDJL2.
source: Mutations in KIF22 dominantly cause SEMDJL2, and patients with both de novo and inherited mutations have been identified (Boyden et al., 2011; Min et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Patients with both de novo and inherited KIF22 mutations have been identified.
source: Mutations in KIF22 dominantly cause SEMDJL2, and patients with both de novo and inherited mutations have been identified (Boyden et al., 2011; Min et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: KIF22 mRNA is expressed throughout the body.
source: Although KIF22 mRNA is expressed throughout the body (Human Protein Atlas; http://www.proteinatlas.org; Uhlén et al., 2015), the effects of these mutations are largely tissue-specific, and the development of the skeletal system is most affected in SEMDJL2 patients.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to the Human Protein Atlas.

claim: The effects of KIF22 mutations are largely tissue-specific, and the development of the skeletal system is most affected in SEMDJL2 patients.
source: Although KIF22 mRNA is expressed throughout the body (Human Protein Atlas; http://www.proteinatlas.org; Uhlén et al., 2015), the effects of these mutations are largely tissue-specific, and the development of the skeletal system is most affected in SEMDJL2 patients.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is consistent with clinical descriptions of SEMDJL2 patients.

claim: A primary symptom of SEMDJL2 is short stature, resulting from shortening of both the trunk and the limbs.
source: A primary symptom of SEMDJL2 is short stature, resulting from shortening of both the trunk and the limbs.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is consistent with clinical descriptions of SEMDJL2 patients.

claim: SEMDJL2 patients present with joint laxity, midface hypoplasia, scoliosis, and leptodactyly.
source: Additionally, patients presented with joint laxity, midface hypoplasia, scoliosis, and leptodactyly, a narrowing of the fingers (Boyden et al., 2011; Min et al., 2011).

claim: In very young children with SEMDJL2, the softness of the cartilage in the larynx and trachea caused respiratory issues.
source: In very young children with SEMDJL2, the softness of the cartilage in the larynx and trachea caused respiratory issues (Boyden et al., 2011).

source: Growth plate radiology demonstrated delayed maturation of the metaphyses and epiphyses in SEMDJL2 patients, and symptoms became more pronounced as patients aged (Tüysüz et al., 2015).

source: Leptodactyly, specifically, was only observed in older (young adult) patients (Boyden et al., 2011).

claim: KIF22 knockout in mice did not affect skeletal development.
source: However, KIF22 knockout in mice did not affect skeletal development.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is consistent with prior work on KIF22 knockout mice.

source: Loss of KIF22 was lethal early in embryogenesis for approximately 50% of embryos, but mice that survived past this point developed to adulthood and demonstrated no gross abnormalities or pathologies (Ohsugi et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to Ohsugi et al., 2003.

claim: Mice that survived past early embryogenesis developed to adulthood and demonstrated no gross abnormalities or pathologies.
source: Loss of KIF22 was lethal early in embryogenesis for approximately 50% of embryos, but mice that survived past this point developed to adulthood and demonstrated no gross abnormalities or pathologies (Ohsugi et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to Ohsugi et al., 2003.

source: This gain of function phenotype is consistent with a lack of KIF22 inactivation in anaphase, resulting in a failure to suspend polar ejection force generation.

claim: The percentage of cells with abnormally shaped nuclei was increased in cells expressing KIF22-GFP T158D in the presence (36%) or absence (32%) of endogenous KIF22.
source: Mimicking phosphorylation of T158 also affected daughter cell nuclear morphology. evidence: This is stated in the results section. Figure 9I shows quantification of the percentage of cells with abnormally shaped nuclei in cells expressing KIF22-GFP T158D.

claim: The expression of KIF22-GFP T158D phenocopies the expression of KIF22-GFP T463D or KIF22-GFP with pathogenic mutations, suggesting that dephosphorylation of T158 contributes to KIF22 inactivation in anaphase.
source: The expression of KIF22-GFP T158D phenocopies the expression of KIF22-GFP T463D or KIF22-GFP with pathogenic mutations, suggesting that dephosphorylation of T158 contributes to KIF22 inactivation in anaphase.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and is inferred from the observation that KIF22-GFP T158D causes anaphase chromosome recongression and nuclear morphology defects similar to those seen with pathogenic mutations and KIF22-GFP T463D.

claim: Immunoprecipitation (IP) was performed to test for interaction between Motor Domain-GFP and mCh-Tail 442–506 or mCh-Tail 420–520. Motor Domain-GFP was detected in samples after anti-GFP IP, but neither mCh-Tail 442–506 nor mCh-Tail 420–520 co-immunoprecipitated with Motor Domain-GFP.

evidence: This is stated in the results section. Figure 9—figure supplement 3D shows a western blot of IP samples.

claim: Pathogenic mutations result in a gain of KIF22 function, which aligns with findings that KIF22 mutations are dominant in heterozygous patients.
source: Thus, we conclude that pathogenic mutations result in a gain of KIF22 function, which aligns with findings that KIF22 mutations are dominant in heterozygous patients (Boyden et al., 2011; Min et al., 2011; Tüysüz et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is supported by experimental data showing that mutant KIF22 causes anaphase chromosome recongression and nuclear morphology defects.

claim: The effects of pathogenic mutations on chromosome movements in anaphase are consistent with observations of chromosome recongression in cells with altered CDK1 activity or altered tail structure.
source: The effects of pathogenic mutations on chromosome movements in anaphase are consistent with observations of chromosome recongression in cells with altered CDK1 activity (Su et al., 2016; Wolf et al., 2006) or altered tail structure (Soeda et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Mutations in both the motor domain (P148L, P148S, R149L, and R149Q) and the coiled-coil domain (V475G) of KIF22 disrupt chromosome segregation in a manner consistent with a failure of KIF22 inactivation in anaphase.
source: Mutations in both the motor domain (P148L, P148S, R149L, and R149Q) and the coiled-coil domain (V475G) of KIF22 disrupt chromosome segregation in a manner consistent with a failure of KIF22 inactivation in anaphase.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is supported by experimental data showing that all tested pathogenic mutations cause anaphase chromosome recongression.

claim: Mimicking phosphorylation of T158 in the motor domain or T463 in the tail also disrupts chromosome segregation.
source: Additionally, mimicking phosphorylation of T158 in the motor domain or T463 in the tail also disrupts chromosome segregation.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is supported by experimental data showing that KIF22-GFP T158D and T463D cause anaphase chromosome recongression.

claim: These findings demonstrate that the motor domain α2 helix participates in the process of KIF22 inactivation.
source: These findings demonstrate that the motor domain α2 helix participates in the process of KIF22 inactivation, adding to studies that demonstrate that deletion of the tail microtubule-binding domain and deletion or disruption of the coiled-coil domain prevent the inactivation of KIF22 in anaphase (Soeda et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is supported by experimental data showing that mutations in the α2 helix and mimicking phosphorylation of T158 disrupt anaphase chromosome segregation.

claim: Phosphorylation of KIF22 T158 has been detected in mitotic cells, but the relative phosphorylation levels of this residue at different times in mitosis are not known.
source: Phosphorylation of KIF22 T158 has been detected in mitotic cells, but the relative phosphorylation levels of this residue at different times in mitosis are not known (Olsen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is supported by a citation to Olsen et al., 2010.

claim: The physical mechanism of KIF22 inactivation is unknown.
source: The physical mechanism of KIF22 inactivation is unknown, and our results can be interpreted in the context of several models, which are not mutually exclusive.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion.

claim: Previous work has proposed that the tail of KIF22 may interact with microtubules to suspend polar ejection force generation, as KIF22 inactivation requires the tail second microtubule-binding and coiled-coil domains.
source: Previous work has proposed that the tail of KIF22 may interact with microtubules to suspend polar ejection force generation, as KIF22 inactivation requires the tail second microtubule-binding and coiled-coil domains (Soeda et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is supported by a citation to Soeda et al., 2016.

claim: Head-tail autoinhibition is a known regulatory mechanism of other members of the kinesin superfamily.
source: Alternatively, given that mutations in the tail and motor domain of KIF22 both disrupt chromosome segregation, the tail and motor domain may interact to inactivate the motor. Head-tail autoinhibition is a known regulatory mechanism of other members of the kinesin superfamily (Blasius et al., 2021; Coy et al., 1999; Espeut et al., 2008; Friedman and Vale, 1999; Hammond et al., 2010; Hammond et al., 2009; Imanishi et al., 2006; Ren et al., 2018; Verhey and Hammond, 2009; Verhey et al., 1998), and disruption of autoinhibition can be a mechanism of disease pathogenesis (Asselin et al., 2020; Bianchi et al., 2016; Blasius et al., 2021; Cheng et al., 2014; Pant et al., 2022; van der Vaart et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Disruption of autoinhibition can be a mechanism of disease pathogenesis.
source: Alternatively, given that mutations in the tail and motor domain of KIF22 both disrupt chromosome segregation, the tail and motor domain may interact to inactivate the motor. Head-tail autoinhibition is a known regulatory mechanism of other members of the kinesin superfamily (Blasius et al., 2021; Coy et al., 1999; Espeut et al., 2008; Friedman and Vale, 1999; Hammond et al., 2010; Hammond et al., 2009; Imanishi et al., 2006; Ren et al., 2018; Verhey and Hammond, 2009; Verhey et al., 1998), and disruption of autoinhibition can be a mechanism of disease pathogenesis (Asselin et al., 2020; Bianchi et al., 2016; Blasius et al., 2021; Cheng et al., 2014; Pant et al., 2022; van der Vaart et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: An allosteric mechanism by which conformational changes are propagated down the stalk to the motor domain has recently been proposed to contribute to the inactivation of kinesin-1 motors by kinesin light chain, which binds the tail.
source: An allosteric mechanism by which conformational changes are propagated down the stalk to the motor domain has recently been proposed to contribute to the inactivation of kinesin-1 motors by kinesin light chain, which binds the tail (Chiba et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is supported by a citation to Chiba et al., 2021.

claim: Addition of a phosphonull T463A mutation to KIF22 with coiled-coil or microtubule-binding domain deletions does not rescue anaphase chromosome recongression defects, suggesting that the role of the KIF22 tail in motor inactivation is not only to facilitate dephosphorylation of T463.
source: However, addition of a phosphonull T463A mutation to KIF22 with coiled-coil or microtubule-binding domain deletions does not rescue anaphase chromosome recongression defects (Soeda et al., 2016), suggesting that the role of the KIF22 tail in motor inactivation is not only to facilitate dephosphorylation of T463.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is supported by a citation to Soeda et al., 2016.

claim: The regulation of the motor domain α2 helix in KIF22 inactivation may inform our understanding of additional kinesin motors, as amino acids P148 and R149 are conserved in a number of members of the kinesin superfamily.
source: The regulation of the motor domain α2 helix in KIF22 inactivation may inform our understanding of additional kinesin motors, as amino acids P148 and R149 are conserved in a number of members of the kinesin superfamily (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion. Figure 1D shows sequence alignments demonstrating conservation of P148 and R149 in human kinesin superfamily members.

claim: Phosphorylation or acetylation of amino acids in the α2 helix has been reported for members of the kinesin-3 (KIF13A S134), kinesin-5 (KIF11 Y125, K146), kinesin-6 (KIF20B S182 and KIF23 S125), and kinesin-14 (KIFC3 S557) families.
source: Similarly, phosphorylation or acetylation of amino acids in the α2 helix has been reported for members of the kinesin-3 (KIF13A S134) (Dephoure et al., 2008), kinesin-5 (KIF11 Y125, K146) (Bickel et al., 2017; Choudhary et al., 2009), kinesin-6 (KIF20B S182 and KIF23 S125) (Hegemann et al., 2011; Sharma et al., 2014; Shiromizu et al., 2013), and kinesin-14 (KIFC3 S557) (Sharma et al., 2014) families.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is supported by citations to prior work.

source: Phosphorylation of Y125 (Bickel et al., 2017) and acetylation of K146 (Muretta et al., 2018) in KIF11 (Eg5) have been shown to modulate motor activity, and the functions of the remaining reported post-translation modifications in the α2 helix are yet to be characterized.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Acetylation of KIF11 at K146 increases the stall force of the motor and slows anaphase spindle pole separation.
source: Acetylation of KIF11 at K146 increases the stall force of the motor and slows anaphase spindle pole separation (Muretta et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is supported by a citation to Muretta et al., 2018.

evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is consistent with live-cell imaging data.

claim: These dynamics may be due to differences in microtubule density closer to the poles compared to the center of the spindle.

evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is a speculative interpretation of the observed chromosome dynamics.

source: This model is consistent with work demonstrating that in monopolar spindles, poleward movement of chromosomes is limited by chromosomes reaching a threshold density of microtubules at which polar ejection forces are sufficient to cause chromosomes to switch to anti-poleward movement (Cassimeris et al., 1994).

evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is consistent with live-cell imaging data.

claim: This could be explained by the central chromosomes encountering a higher density of microtubules, and KIF22 bound to these chromosomes therefore generating higher levels of polar ejection forces.
source: This could also be explained by the central chromosomes encountering a higher density of microtubules, and KIF22 bound to these chromosomes therefore generating higher levels of polar ejection forces.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is a speculative interpretation of the observed chromosome dynamics.

source: Expression of KIF22-GFP with pathogenic mutations did not alter the distance between centromeres and spindle poles, indicating that while anaphase polar ejection forces altered the position of chromosome arms within the spindle, these forces were not sufficient to prevent the shortening of k-fibers.

source: This suggests that the polar ejection forces collectively generated by mutant KIF22 motors are of greater magnitude than the forces sliding the spindle poles apart during anaphase B.

evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is inferred from the observation that mutant KIF22 affects both chromosome arm movements and spindle pole separation.
